topic: Vasopressors & Septic Shock — Restoring Perfusion Pressure
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Critical Care Unit
speakerBio: An intensivist who teaches haemodynamics at the bedside — famous for the mantra 'pressure is not perfusion' and for making trainees put the echo probe down only after they can explain the number.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

A 68-year-old woman with urosepsis is in front of you. She has had 30 mL/kg of crystalloid over the last hour, her lactate is 4.8, and her arterial line reads MAP 52. She is warm, flushed, and her hands are bounding — this is not a pump that has failed, it is a circuit that has lost its tone. Fluid alone will not fix a dilated arterial tree. This session is about the drugs that put the squeeze back into the vessels, in what order, at what target, and why.

1 · The mechanism first — why the vessels let go 🫀

Septic shock is fundamentally a distributive problem. The invading organism and the host response flood the endothelium with mediators — nitric oxide (via inducible NO synthase), prostacyclin, and others — that relax vascular smooth muscle. The result is a vicious cycle:

  1. Vasodilation → the arterial tree that normally holds pressure becomes a floppy, over-large container.
  2. The same container now holds the same blood volume at a lower pressure → MAP falls.
  3. Capillary leak moves fluid out of the vessels → relative and absolute hypovolaemia stack on top of the vasodilation.
  4. Perfusion pressure to kidney, gut and brain falls below the threshold each organ needs → organ injury, rising lactate, worsening acidosis.
  5. Acidosis itself blunts adrenoreceptor responsiveness → the vessels respond less to your drugs → you chase the pressure higher and higher.

The vasopressor's job is to interrupt this cycle at step 1: to restore vascular tone and therefore perfusion pressure, buying the antibiotics and source control time to work.

💡 One-liner

Sepsis is a tank, a pump and pipes problem — but septic shock is mostly a PIPES problem. Fill the tank first, then tighten the pipes; only rarely do you need to help the pump.

2 · Noradrenaline — the undisputed first-line 🥇

Noradrenaline (norepinephrine) is the first-choice vasopressor in septic shock (Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021, strong recommendation). It is a potent α₁-adrenergic agonist — α₁ stimulation triggers vascular smooth-muscle contraction, directly reversing the pathological vasodilation. It has modest β₁ activity that supports stroke volume and heart rate without the runaway tachycardia of pure β-agonists.

  • Why it wins: raises MAP reliably by increasing systemic vascular resistance, with less tachyarrhythmia than dopamine or adrenaline and a neutral-to-favourable effect on splanchnic and renal perfusion.
  • Starting dose: typically 0.05–0.1 µg/kg/min, titrated to the MAP target. There is no fixed ceiling — titrate to effect — but a persistent requirement above ~0.5 µg/kg/min is your cue to add a second agent, not simply to keep climbing.

The target — MAP ≥ 65 mmHg 🎯

The default resuscitation target is a MAP of at least 65 mmHg. This is the pressure below which autoregulation in most vascular beds fails and flow becomes pressure-dependent.

🎯 Contrast — one target does not fit all

The SEPSISPAM trial randomised patients to a MAP target of 65–70 vs 80–85 mmHg. Overall mortality was the same, but the chronically hypertensive subgroup had less need for renal replacement therapy at the higher target — their kidneys are used to perfusing at a higher pressure. The higher-target group also had more atrial fibrillation. Lesson: default to ≥65, but individualise UP for the patient with long-standing hypertension, and do not chase supranormal pressures in everyone.

3 · The order of battle — how to escalate 🪜

StepAgentDose / detailRationale
1st lineNoradrenalineTitrate to MAP ≥65Potent α₁ vasoconstriction, favourable side-effect profile
2nd agentVasopressinFixed 0.03 U/min (not titrated)Catecholamine-sparing; restores a hormone that is deficient in shock
3rd lineAdrenaline (epinephrine)Titrate; add or substituteExtra α + β when MAP still inadequate
RefractoryAngiotensin IITitrate (where available)Non-catecholamine pressor via renin–angiotensin axis
Pump problemDobutamine2.5–20 µg/kg/minInotrope for sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy (see §6)

4 · Vasopressin — sparing the catecholamines 💧

When noradrenaline requirements climb (SSC suggests adding at roughly 0.25–0.5 µg/kg/min of noradrenaline), add vasopressin at a fixed 0.03 U/min. Vasopressin (ADH) acts on V₁ receptors on vascular smooth muscle — a completely different receptor from the adrenoreceptors — so it constricts vessels even when adrenergic responsiveness is blunted by acidosis. Endogenous vasopressin is paradoxically deficient in established septic shock, so this is partly replacement of a missing hormone.

  • It is catecholamine-sparing: adding vasopressin lets you pull back the noradrenaline dose, reducing catecholamine-driven tachyarrhythmia, myocardial oxygen demand and immunomodulatory harm.
  • The VASST trial showed vasopressin added to noradrenaline was not superior overall, but in the less-severe shock subgroup there was a mortality signal in its favour — reinforcing "add early as a second agent," not "wait until the patient is nearly dead."
  • Do not titrate it and do not exceed 0.03–0.04 U/min — higher doses cause digital, splanchnic and coronary ischaemia.
⚠️ Danger — vasopressin is a fixed dose

Vasopressin is not a rescue knob you crank up when the pressure drops. It is added at 0.03 U/min and left there. If you titrate it like noradrenaline you will produce mesenteric and digital ischaemia. Escalate the adrenaline, not the vasopressin.

5 · Adrenaline and angiotensin II — the later lines ⚡

Adrenaline (epinephrine) is the third-line agent — added when MAP remains inadequate on noradrenaline plus vasopressin. It has powerful α and β effects. The trade-off is more tachycardia, more arrhythmia, and a transient rise in lactate (β₂-driven aerobic glycolysis), which can muddy your lactate-clearance readings — anticipate it rather than mistaking it for worsening hypoperfusion.

Angiotensin II is a non-catecholamine vasopressor acting through the renin–angiotensin system. The ATHOS-3 trial showed it reliably raised MAP in catecholamine-refractory vasodilatory shock and allowed background catecholamine doses to be reduced. It is an option for the truly refractory patient where available.

6 · The pump can fail too — dobutamine for septic cardiomyopathy 🫀

Around 10–20% of septic patients develop sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy — a reversible, biventricular systolic (and diastolic) dysfunction driven by circulating myocardial depressant mediators. The clue: despite adequate filling and an adequate MAP on noradrenaline, the patient stays hypoperfused — mottled, oliguric, rising lactate, low ScvO₂ — and echo shows a poorly contracting, dilated ventricle.

Here you add an inotrope: dobutamine 2.5–20 µg/kg/min (a β₁ agonist that increases contractility and cardiac output). SSC 2021 suggests adding dobutamine (or switching to adrenaline) for persistent hypoperfusion despite adequate volume and MAP.

💡 Pearl — pressure is not the same as flow

A normal MAP with cold mottled skin, oliguria and a climbing lactate is a flow problem, not a pressure problem. That is when you reach for the echo probe and consider an inotrope — do not just keep turning up the noradrenaline.

7 · Access — you do not have to wait for a central line 🩸

Classic teaching said vasopressors demand central access because of extravasation necrosis. Current practice: start noradrenaline peripherally through a good, proximal, well-sited large-bore cannula while you obtain central access — do not let the patient sit hypotensive waiting for a CVC. SSC 2021 supports early peripheral initiation for a short period.

  • Use a proximal vein (antecubital or larger), not the hand or foot.
  • Monitor the site closely for extravasation; have phentolamine available for infiltration.
  • Transition to a central line within hours, especially for higher doses or prolonged need.

8 · Corticosteroids in refractory shock 💊

Persistent shock despite adequate fluids and vasopressors is the trigger to add hydrocortisone 200 mg/day (as 50 mg IV every 6 hours, or a continuous infusion). The rationale is relative adrenal insufficiency and restoration of vascular responsiveness to catecholamines.

TrialRegimenPunchline
APROCCHSSHydrocortisone 50 mg q6h + fludrocortisoneLower 90-day mortality in septic shock
ADRENALHydrocortisone 200 mg/day infusionNo mortality difference, but faster shock reversal, faster weaning off pressors and ventilator
SSC 2021Suggests IV hydrocortisone 200 mg/dayFor adults with ongoing vasopressor requirement (≈≥0.25 µg/kg/min noradrenaline ≥4 h)

The consistent, undisputed finding across both landmark trials is faster shock reversal — you get your patient off pressors sooner. Reserve it for the vasopressor-dependent patient, not every septic patient.

9 · The contrast that matters — noradrenaline vs dopamine ⚔️

🎯 Why dopamine lost

Dopamine was once first-line and was believed to have a protective "renal-dose" effect. Both claims collapsed. In the landmark De Backer 2010 trial (noradrenaline vs dopamine in shock), dopamine caused significantly more arrhythmias, and in the cardiogenic shock subgroup it caused higher mortality. "Renal-dose" dopamine does not protect kidneys. Noradrenaline is first-line; dopamine is a downgraded, second-tier option reserved for highly selected bradycardic patients at low arrhythmia risk.

☠️ M&M — the pressure that was chased instead of the pump

A 59-year-old man with pneumonia and septic shock was on noradrenaline at 0.9 µg/kg/min. His MAP was 66 — "at target" — but he was mottled to the knees, anuric, and his lactate had climbed from 4 to 7. The overnight team, focused only on the arterial line number, kept escalating noradrenaline toward 1.4 µg/kg/min. His heart rate hit 150 and he threw a run of VT. Morning echo showed a dilated, barely-contracting left ventricle — sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy. He had a flow problem masquerading as an adequate pressure, and the relentless α-agonism was flogging a failing heart into arrhythmia. Lesson: when the MAP is at target but the patient stays hypoperfused, stop cranking the pressor — put the probe on, add vasopressin to spare catecholamines, and reach for an inotrope. Pressure is not perfusion.

10 · Take-home 📌

  • Noradrenaline first — α₁ vasoconstriction reverses the collapsed vascular tone; target MAP ≥65, individualise UP in chronic hypertension (SEPSISPAM).
  • Add vasopressin 0.03 U/min (fixed, never titrated) as the second agent to spare catecholamines.
  • Adrenaline third; angiotensin II for refractory shock.
  • Start pressors peripherally through a proximal large vein while central access is obtained.
  • Dobutamine for sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy — pressure at target but still hypoperfused = flow problem.
  • Hydrocortisone 200 mg/day in vasopressor-refractory shock (APROCCHSS, ADRENAL — faster shock reversal).
  • Dopamine is out — more arrhythmia, worse mortality; noradrenaline wins.

moderatorQs.q: Your patient is fluid-resuscitated but the MAP is 54. What is your first drug, your target, and how do you individualise it?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Noradrenaline is first-line (SSC 2021, strong recommendation) — a potent α₁ agonist that reverses the pathological vasodilation of distributive shock with less arrhythmia than dopamine or adrenaline. I titrate to a MAP of ≥65 mmHg, the default target below which autoregulation fails. I individualise upward — toward 80–85 — in a chronically hypertensive patient, because the SEPSISPAM trial showed that subgroup needed less renal replacement therapy at the higher target. I do not chase supranormal pressures in everyone, since the higher target also caused more atrial fibrillation.

moderatorQs.q: Noradrenaline is at 0.5 µg/kg/min and climbing. Why add vasopressin rather than just turning up the noradrenaline?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Because vasopressin acts through a completely different receptor — the V₁ receptor on vascular smooth muscle — so it constricts vessels even when acidosis has blunted the adrenoreceptors, and endogenous vasopressin is paradoxically deficient in established shock. It is added at a fixed 0.03 U/min and is catecholamine-sparing: it lets me pull back the noradrenaline, reducing catecholamine-driven tachyarrhythmia and myocardial oxygen demand. Crucially it is not titrated — cranking it up causes digital and mesenteric ischaemia.

moderatorQs.q: Why did dopamine fall out of favour as a first-line vasopressor?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: The De Backer 2010 trial comparing dopamine with noradrenaline in shock showed dopamine caused significantly more arrhythmias, and in the cardiogenic-shock subgroup it caused higher mortality. The old belief in a protective 'renal-dose' dopamine effect was also debunked — it does not protect kidneys. So noradrenaline is first-line, and dopamine is a downgraded option reserved only for highly selected bradycardic patients with low arrhythmia risk.

audienceQs.q: The MAP is 68 on noradrenaline but the patient is mottled, anuric and the lactate is rising. What now?
audienceQs.answerHTML: That is a flow problem, not a pressure problem — do not just escalate the noradrenaline. Put the echo probe on: you are likely looking at sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy, a reversible biventricular systolic dysfunction seen in 10–20% of septic patients. Add an inotrope — dobutamine 2.5–20 µg/kg/min (or switch toward adrenaline) to restore cardiac output, as SSC 2021 suggests for persistent hypoperfusion despite adequate volume and MAP. Pressure at target does not mean the tissues are being perfused.

audienceQs.q: Do I really have to wait for a central line before starting noradrenaline?
audienceQs.answerHTML: No. Current practice (SSC 2021) is to start noradrenaline peripherally through a good, proximal, large-bore cannula — antecubital or bigger, never the hand or foot — while central access is being obtained, rather than leaving the patient dangerously hypotensive. Watch the site closely for extravasation, keep phentolamine available for infiltration, and transition to a central line within a few hours, especially for higher doses.

audienceQs.q: When do steroids get added, and at what dose?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Add hydrocortisone 200 mg/day — as 50 mg IV every 6 hours or a continuous infusion — for shock that remains vasopressor-dependent despite adequate fluids and noradrenaline (roughly ≥0.25 µg/kg/min for ≥4 hours). The evidence is APROCCHSS (lower 90-day mortality with hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone) and ADRENAL (no mortality change but faster shock reversal and quicker weaning off pressors). It is for the refractory patient, not routine sepsis.
